cf.title: Report changes discarded for relations not in the subscription

input.subject: [PATCH] Report changes discarded for relations not in the subscription

verdict_reasoning: Nothing that survived stops the proposal at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated with a field case, apply behavior does not change, and only subscribers that hit the condition see the new messages. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is a fixable design point: the commit message names a missing conflict and statistics counter, and v2 adds neither. Nobody has commented on the design in the thread yet.

brief.title: Log changes the apply worker discards for relations not in the subscription
brief.problem: The apply worker silently discards changes for a relation that is not in SUBREL_STATE_READY, while the replication origin and the publisher slot advance past them. A table with no pg_subscription_rel row, such as one added to a publication without REFRESH PUBLICATION, loses those rows for good. Subscriber administrators cannot see this or tell it from an ongoing table sync.
brief.proposed_design: should_apply_changes_for_rel() reports the skip, at LOG with a REFRESH PUBLICATION hint when the relation is not in the subscription, and at DEBUG2 when it is not yet synchronized. Each relation is reported once per sync state for the life of the apply worker, tracked in LogicalRepRelMapEntry. Apply behavior does not change, and v2 drops the v1 throttle based on wal_retrieve_retry_interval.
user_visible_surface: New LOG message: skipping changes for relation "..." in subscription "...", with DETAIL that the relation is not part of the subscription and a HINT to run ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH PUBLICATION.
New DEBUG2 message for changes skipped because the relation is not yet synchronized.
New field in LogicalRepRelMapEntry (logicalrelation.h), visible to C code that uses this struct.
author_claims: Today the discard leaves no log message at any level, no conflict and no statistics counter.
The new messages let a user tell a lost table list apart from a missing REFRESH PUBLICATION.
No behavior change beyond the new messages.
Each relation is reported once per sync state, so the log does not get one message per row.
The patch is for master only because it changes LogicalRepRelMapEntry.
brief.thread_state: Hayato Kuroda asked for the upgrade versions and noted that pg_upgrade keeps pg_subscription_rel since 9a17be1e2 for PG17+; the author answered 14 to 18. No one has replied to v2, and no one has commented on the design.
unclear: The thread does not say whether the empty pg_subscription_rel after a 14-to-18 pg_upgrade is expected or a bug to fix separately.
The proposal does not say whether a LOG message is the right level for a condition that repeats after every apply worker restart.
The proposal does not explain why it adds no statistics counter or conflict type, given the problem statement names both as missing.
The thread does not say how a parallel apply worker shares or repeats the once-per-state tracking with the leader.
The patch prose shows no documentation change about this case in the logical replication chapter.
search_queries: apply worker relation not in subscription

prior_attempts.title: Apply worker fails if a relation is missing on subscriber even if refresh publication has not been refreshed yet
prior_attempts.quote: I see your point but not sure if it is worth changing the current behavior without any specific use case which we want to address with this change.
prior_attempts.reason: Amit Kapila questioned whether the current ERROR behavior should be changed when no specific use case had been given. He noted that users can avoid the failure loop with the disable_on_error subscription parameter, and that silently skipping changes could surprise users whose subscriber-side setup is incomplete. The author said he had no specific use case, and the entry was withdrawn.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 changed apply behavior, replacing an ERROR with a warning and a skip when a table was missing on the subscriber, and gave no use case. This proposal changes no behavior, only logs a skip that already happens silently, and gives a field case in message #1.

objections.title: Ad hoc LOG line where conflict logging and subscription stats exist
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring setup that tracks apply problems through pg_stat_subscription_stats sees no counter move while rows for an unrefreshed table are discarded. The single LOG line per worker lifetime is easy to miss in log rotation. The administrator finds the loss only when the subscriber table is compared with the publisher.
objections.argument: Postgres already reports apply-side anomalies through conflict types that are logged with a fixed format and counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats. The commit message names the missing counter and the missing conflict as part of the problem, but v2 adds neither. It adds a free-form message reported once per relation and sync state, so the log shows no ongoing count of discarded changes. A committer would likely ask why the existing reporting mechanism does not fit this case, or why it is deferred.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a once-per-worker LOG message preferred over a pg_stat_subscription_stats counter or a conflict type for permanently discarded changes?

critic.reasoning: The commit message names the missing conflict and statistics counter as part of the problem, and v2 adds neither. No message in the thread says why a once-per-worker LOG message is preferred over pg_stat_subscription_stats.

refuted.title: One LOG line per worker lifetime is a weak signal for permanent loss
refuted.failure_scenario: A subscriber's apply worker runs for weeks and logs the skip once on its first change. The log rotates, and the worker keeps discarding rows for that table with no further trace. A monitoring system that reads pg_stat_subscription_stats sees nothing and never alerts.
refuted.argument: The problem statement in message #4 names three missing things: a log message, a conflict and a statistics counter. The patch adds only the first. pg_stat_subscription_stats already carries per-subscription error and conflict counters, and that view is where administrators look for apply problems. A one-time message keyed to process lifetime gives no count and no ongoing signal, and a later patch that adds a counter would replace or duplicate this one.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is a one-time LOG message enough, and why not a skipped-changes counter in pg_stat_subscription_stats that survives log rotation and worker restarts?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Both ask why the patch adds a one-time LOG message and no counter in pg_stat_subscription_stats.

refuted.title: A catalog comparison already finds tables missing from the subscription
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator who wants to catch a missed REFRESH PUBLICATION can already compare pg_publication_tables on the publisher with pg_subscription_rel on the subscriber. That check catches both the empty catalog after the 14-to-18 upgrade and a table added without a refresh. The new LOG line fires only after changes for the table arrive, so it reports the problem later than the check does.
refuted.argument: Both cases in messages #1 and #4 come down to a published table with no pg_subscription_rel row, and existing catalogs can show that. The proposal does not mention this check. It also does not explain why a log line, which needs log scraping, is better than a periodic query or a counter in pg_stat_subscription_stats. The author's point that the server cannot tell the two cases apart holds only from inside the apply worker; a monitoring query that joins both nodes can.
refuted.author_must_show: Which failure does a comparison of pg_publication_tables with pg_subscription_rel miss, other than the extra effort of querying both nodes, that the new LOG message catches?

critic.reasoning: The scenario describes an alternative check and names no harm from the new message. That check needs access to both nodes and an administrator who already suspects a missed refresh, while the message reaches those who do not; the counter point duplicates standards-compat-1.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch adds reporting to the logical replication apply worker in worker.c; apply behavior stays the same.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a field to LogicalRepRelMapEntry in logicalrelation.h, which C code can see.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The author limits the patch to master because it changes LogicalRepRelMapEntry, so released branches keep the silent discard.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a user-visible LOG message with a hint, plus once-per-state tracking in the relation map entry.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: should_apply_changes_for_rel() runs once per applied change, and the new check sits in it.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Why is a LOG message reported once per apply worker lifetime preferred over a pg_stat_subscription_stats counter or a conflict type for permanently discarded changes?
Is the empty pg_subscription_rel after a 14-to-18 pg_upgrade expected, or is it a bug that needs a separate fix?
Is LOG the intended level for a message that repeats for each affected relation after every apply worker restart?
Does a parallel apply worker share the once-per-state tracking with the leader, or does each worker report the same relation again?
Will the logical replication chapter document that changes for a published table are discarded until REFRESH PUBLICATION runs?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows the logical replication apply worker and table synchronization code would have to own it. None has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: Small: the wording and level of one LOG message that users may come to rely on, plus the once-per-state tracking in the relation map entry. A later counter or conflict type could make the message redundant.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the reviewer's question within a day and posted v2 (message #4).

priority.reason: The patch is about 11 KiB, touches worker.c, one header and two TAP tests, and makes a permanent silent discard visible to logical replication users. The open point in standards-compat-1 can be settled in normal review.

provisional_note: Without the code, we could not check the cost of the new check per change, how the tracking survives relation map invalidation, or what parallel apply workers report.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: skip empty transactions for logical replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change pgoutput so it defers the BEGIN message until a transaction produces a change to send, and drops BEGIN and COMMIT for transactions that touch no published tables. The goal is to cut network traffic when most upstream transactions only modify unpublished tables.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding. The patch no longer applied and stayed in Waiting on Author for about six weeks, so it was marked Returned with feedback. Open design questions were never resolved: Craig Ringer noted that skipping empty transactions can delay synchronous replication feedback, and Andres Freund proposed a lighter progress message or rate limiting instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since then, the patch is failing to apply, waiting on author and the thread has died 6 weeks or so ago, so I am marking it as RwF in the CF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert logical snapshot filename format change in SnapBuildSnapshotExists().
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert logical snapshot filename format change in SnapBuildSnapshotExists().
Reverted commit(s): Standardize LSN formatting by zero padding
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 2633dae2e48 standardized LSN formatting but mistakenly changed
the logical snapshot filename format in SnapBuildSnapshotExists() from
"%X-%X.snap" to "%08X-%08X.snap". Other code still used the original
"%X-%X.snap" format, causing the replication slot synchronization worker
to fail to find existing snapshot files and produce excessive log messages.

This commit restores the original "%X-%X.snap" format
in SnapBuildSnapshotExists() to resolve the issue.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reuse Workers and Replication Slots during Logical Replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a tablesync worker, after it finishes one table, pick up the next table in init state and sync it, keeping its replication slot. This removes the cost of starting a new worker and creating and dropping a slot for each table, which matters most for many empty or small tables.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks by reviewers showed regressions in some settings, and the v28 design #2 results were up to about twice as slow as HEAD and varied widely between runs. The patch also no longer applied to HEAD. Amit Kapila proposed Returned with feedback because the regressions still needed analysis, and vignesh C asked for a new entry with a fix for the regression.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
IIRC, there were some regressions observed with this patch. So, one
needs to analyze those as well.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical replication timeout
precedents_retrieved.summary: A walsender spent hours unlinking every possible spill file name for a large transaction in ReorderBufferRestoreCleanup, so the subscriber timed out and decoding restarted in a loop. The patch records which WAL segments a transaction actually spilled to, so cleanup removes only those files.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message, in March 2025, only reports a rebase. A reviewer had also asked for a second patch that sends progress updates during long loops such as cleanup, and no message shows that patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical Replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: Petr Jelinek posted a WIP patch set for built-in logical replication, with publication and subscription catalogs and DDL, a logical replication protocol and output plugin, and apply workers started by a launcher. It also included a proof-of-concept initial data copy, and left out sequences, DDL replication, TRUNCATE, ACLs and full pg_dump support.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The CF manager returned the entry because the newest patch was three weeks old while review was still ongoing. Peter Eisentraut had posted detailed reviews of each patch, Steve Singer had reported bugs such as a crash in the apply worker after column changes on the subscriber, and no updated version followed. Review found no design objection that blocked the work.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The newest patch is 3-week old, so marking this entry as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: tablesync early exit
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes a tablesync worker call process_syncing_tables() before it enters the apply main loop, so a worker with nothing left to do exits early. The author presented it as a small optimization and as a cleaner split of work between tablesync and apply workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila objected that exiting before the tablesync worker receives any message skips changes up to the LSN where the copy finished. That is safe with the current code but would lose changes for the table in a design where the apply worker applies streamed in-progress transactions, which had already been proposed on -hackers. The saving was only the work to receive messages for one transaction, so the author withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As per my understanding, this is safe as per the current code but it
can't be guaranteed for future implementations and the amount of extra
work is additional work to receive the messages for one transaction.

precedents_retrieved.title: SQL statements statistics counter view (pg_stat_sql)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_sql view that counts SQL statements executed on the instance by command tag, behind a new track_sql GUC, with a reset function. Later versions keep one row per command tag in a hash table, counted in exec_simple_query and exec_execute_message.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback after months without activity, after Alvaro Herrera asked who would rebase it onto the new cmdtaglist.h enum tags. Andres Freund's 2017 review had left open questions: an extension might be the better place, tags should be enums in a fixed array, and counting belongs at the executor level. The author promised an array version, but the visible messages do not show one. A competing cmdstats patch by Mark Dilger also waited on benchmarks that Robert Haas requested.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch had no activity for months, so I am marking it as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Skip replicating the tables specified in except table option
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an EXCEPT TABLE clause to CREATE/ALTER PUBLICATION ... FOR ALL TABLES, which records excluded tables in pg_publication_rel and makes pgoutput skip their changes. A companion patch adds ALTER PUBLICATION ... RESET, which returns a publication to its default state before ALL TABLES with an exception list is added.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after the thread went quiet. From mid-2022 the messages are rebases and commitfest reminders, and the author said he saw little interest from others. Earlier, Peter Eisentraut doubted the feature was worth the trouble and pointed to the cost of tracking negative dependencies. Peter Smith found the meaning of ALTER PUBLICATION combined with EXCEPT ambiguous, but these points did not decide the outcome.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As I did not see much interest from others, I'm withdrawing this patch
for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the work done by commits 3ba59ccc89 and 72e78d831a.
Those commits were incorrect in asserting that we never acquire any other
heavy-weight lock after acquring page lock other than relation extension
lock. We can acquire a lock on catalogs while doing catalog look up after
acquring page lock.

This won't impact any existing feature but we need to think some other way
to achieve this before parallelizing other write operations or even
improving the parallelism in vacuum (like allowing multiple workers
for an index).

precedents_retrieved.title: Replica with large recovery_min_apply_delay is not receiving changes from master after restart until this delay is expired
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Replica with large recovery_min_apply_delay is not receiving changes from master after restart until this delay is expired
Threads: Replication & recovery_min_apply_delay

roaster_notes.note: The one related precedent, [P1], was withdrawn because it changed apply behavior without a use case. This proposal changes no behavior and gives a use case in messages #1 and #4, so that reason does not apply. [P23] covers datatype mismatch warnings and records no reason, and the thread cites no earlier discussion of this idea.
The patch changes no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog or dump format. Apply behaviour stays the same, so existing scripts and dumps are not affected.

The proposal changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol message or replicated state, so pg_upgrade, standbys and subscribers see nothing new. Its only cross-boundary effect is a new field in LogicalRepRelMapEntry; that struct lives only in apply worker memory, and the patch targets master only, so the ABI concern does not apply. Leader and parallel apply workers each keep their own tracking, so a skip may be logged more than once. That costs only extra log lines and loses no state.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect worth objecting to. It writes a qualified relation name and the subscription name to the server log, and apply worker errors already log these. The new messages are limited to one per relation per sync state for each worker lifetime and use the existing relation map entry, so a publisher-side user cannot flood the subscriber log or use unbounded memory beyond what the relation map already uses.

From the maintenance angle the patch is small: one field in a backend-local struct, master only, and a cheap check per change. I see no hot-path, ABI or extension-fit problem worth a separate objection. No committer has replied, so ownership is open, but that is a committability point and not a flaw in the design.
One fixable objection only. No existing feature reports the discard from inside the apply worker. The existing way detects the cause, not the discarded changes.

The problem is real and stated. Adding a table to a publication without REFRESH PUBLICATION is an ordinary step, and today the apply worker drops its changes permanently and silently. The author also reports a production pg_upgrade incident. The cost is one LOG and one DEBUG2 message, and only subscribers that hit the condition pay it. [P1] does not apply: it proposed changing apply behavior, and this patch does not.
